title: The Catholic Church and the papacy
summary: The Catholic Church traces its authority through Jesus to the apostle Peter, regarded as the first pope. The bishop of Rome, considered Peter's successor, was increasingly accepted in the West as head of the whole Church. St Peter's Basilica dates from Constantine in the 4th century. In medieval Europe, about 476 to 1500, the Church dominated religious practice.

uncertainty.note: The institutional papacy crystallized in late antiquity between the late 4th century (c. 380 CE) and the pontificate of Gregory I (c. 590 CE), filling the administrative void left by the Western Roman Empire's collapse in 476 CE.

where.modern_name: Vatican City (Holy See, seat of the Papacy and the central government of the Catholic Church)
where.historical_name: Vatican Hill and Old St. Peter's Basilica, Rome, Western Roman Empire

importance.justification: For over a millennium, the leading religious institution in western Europe.

related.because: Christian origins in Judea and the apostolic missions to Rome laid the theological foundation for the Roman episcopate.

reviewer_note: This outline covers late antiquity and the medieval period only, and the Church continues today. The East did not accept Roman headship; see the East-West Schism record. The pin marks the Vatican.
